title: How Do Graph Signals Affect Recommendation: Unveiling the Mystery of Low and High-Frequency Graph Signals

problem.claim: How low- and high-frequency graph signals affect recommendation remains unresolved.

gap.claim: Existing understanding does not resolve how low- and high-frequency graph signals influence recommendation performance.

contributions.claim: The paper proves that low- and high-frequency graph signals have equivalent effects in recommendation because both smooth similarities between user-item pairs.
It proposes a frequency signal scaler that adjusts the graph signal filter function to fine-tune user-item similarity smoothness and is compatible with any GNN model.
It introduces a space flip method to restore the expressive power of graph embeddings, which the paper states cannot fully capture graph-signal characteristics.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The study shows that effective recommendations can be obtained using only low-frequency or only high-frequency graph signals.
The authors report that extensive experiments on four public datasets validate the effectiveness of their proposed methods.
The authors report that code is available at the supplied GitHub URL.

narrative_sequence.summary: Spectral GNN success in recommendation is often attributed to low-pass filtering, while recent studies emphasize high-frequency signals.
The paper identifies unresolved roles for low- and high-frequency graph signals and investigates their influence on recommendation performance.
It argues theoretically that both frequency ranges equivalently smooth user-item similarities.
It presents a frequency signal scaler and a space flip method to control signal smoothness and recover graph-embedding expressive power.
The authors report effective recommendations using either frequency range alone and validation on four public datasets.

source_observation.claim: The paper reports equivalent recommendation effects for low- and high-frequency signals because both smooth user-item similarities.

interpretation.claim: Recommendation quality may depend more on the resulting similarity smoothness than on a fixed preference for one frequency range.

application.claim: When designing graph-recommendation models, tune signal filtering for the desired user-item similarity smoothness.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify which datasets, tasks, or model conditions limit this interpretation.

source_observation.claim: The authors report that either low-frequency or high-frequency signals alone can support effective recommendations.

interpretation.claim: A recommendation system may not require simultaneous reliance on both frequency ranges.

application.claim: Evaluate single-frequency configurations as candidate baselines or simplified model variants.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when one frequency range is preferable to the other.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide the formal proof details.
The abstract does not identify the four datasets or report quantitative results.
The abstract does not describe the implementation details of either proposed method.
